assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 50,000 messages/s at peak — a mid-tier or crypto venue, not a national equities market (those run 10-100x this). 40% of messages are order entry/cancel; 45% are market-data reads.

assumptions.subject: matcher
assumptions.statement: The matching engine is sharded by symbol range, one single-writer thread per shard, so the two shards' capacities genuinely add (disjoint symbols). 15,000 orders/s per shard is CONSERVATIVE for an in-memory matcher; published single-thread designs reach far higher.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Orders are journaled to the event log synchronously and persisted to PostgreSQL in BATCHES (~20:1), which is why the database sees only ~5% of the order rate. Without that batching a single primary could not absorb 20,000 writes/s.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Keystone's v1 engine is an open queueing network: it models mean throughput and latency, NOT microsecond tail determinism, in-order sequencing or fairness — the properties an exchange is actually judged on. Treat this as a capacity sketch, never a latency guarantee.

assumptions.subject: gateway
assumptions.statement: The order gateway is SELF-HOSTED (FIX/binary session servers), not a managed per-request API gateway; at 50,000 rps a per-request managed service would dominate the bill.

assumptions.subject: compliance
assumptions.statement: Market data, order handling, best execution and audit retention are regulated. Nothing here is a compliance design; expert review is mandatory.

_library.summary: Order-entry gateway, risk checks and a sharded matching engine publishing market data.
